claims.claim: In 2000 the American Academy of Pediatrics issued guidelines recommending that peanut introduction be delayed until age three for at-risk children.
claims.episode_span: The recommendation originated with the American Academy of Pediatrics in 2000.
claims.source_title: From Guidelines to Action: Early Allergen Introduction | Ready. Set. Food!
claims.supporting_quote: the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) issued guidelines in 2000 recommending a delay in introducing peanuts until the age of three. However, the 2000 guidance was not backed by science.

claims.claim: The LEAP trial enrolled 640 high-risk infants aged 4 to 11 months, randomized to peanut consumption or avoidance.
claims.episode_span: a randomized study of 640 high-risk infants conducted in the United Kingdom
claims.source_title: LEAP Study Results (Learning Early About Peanut Allergy)
claims.supporting_quote: LEAP (Learning Early About Peanut allergy) was a randomized controlled clinical trial designed and conducted by the Immune Tolerant Network (ITN) to determine the best strategy to prevent peanut allergy in young children. 640 children between 4 and 11 months of age who were identified as high risk for peanut allergy, based on an existing egg allergy and/or severe eczema, were enrolled in the study.

claims.claim: In LEAP, 17% of avoiders developed peanut allergy by age 5 versus 3% of consumers, and the trial was led from King's College London.
claims.episode_span: Children introduced to peanut products between four and eleven months of age showed an 81 percent reduction in peanut allergy by age five compared with the avoidance group.
claims.source_title: LEAP Study Results (Learning Early About Peanut Allergy)
claims.supporting_quote: The LEAP study, designed and conducted by the ITN with additional support from FARE and led by Professor Gideon Lack at King's College London, is the first randomized trial to prevent food allergy in a large cohort of high-risk infants. Of the children who avoided peanut, 17% developed peanut allergy by the age of 5 years.

claims.claim: The LEAP trial's results showed an 81% reduction in peanut allergies when infants were fed peanut products between 4 and 11 months of age.
claims.episode_span: showed an 81 percent reduction in peanut allergy by age five
claims.source_title: From Guidelines to Action: Early Allergen Introduction | Ready. Set. Food!
claims.supporting_quote: The LEAP trial's results showed an 81% reduction in peanut allergies when infants were fed peanut products between 4 and 11 months of age.

claims.claim: The LEAP trial, by George Du Toit et al., was published in 2015, supported by NIAID, and established that early peanut introduction prevents childhood peanut allergy.

claims.claim: In 2017 NIAID issued revised guidelines recommending early peanut introduction for high-risk infants, a stance the AAP subsequently adopted.
claims.episode_span: the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases issued new interim guidance, and the American Academy of Pediatrics formally reversed its earlier recommendation in 2017
claims.source_title: From Guidelines to Action: Early Allergen Introduction | Ready. Set. Food!
claims.supporting_quote: the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) revised their guidelines in 2017, and started recommending early introduction of peanuts as a preventive measure for high-risk infants. The AAP has since adopted the same stance as the NIAID 2017 guidelines.

claims.claim: US childhood peanut allergy prevalence rose sharply, from about 0.4% in 1997 to more than 2% by 2010.
claims.episode_span: prevalence of peanut allergy among U.S. children roughly tripled, reaching an estimated 2 percent by most population surveys
claims.source_title: Reversing peanut advice prevented tens of thousands of allergy cases, researchers say | NPR Illinois
claims.supporting_quote: In 2015, The New England Journal of Medicine referenced a quadrupling of peanut allergy's prevalence in U.S. children, citing growth from 0.4% in 1997 to more than 2% in 2010.
